camps.name: Home Lake, below Constance Pass — inside the park, and reached from the north
camps.why: Gets you under the northwest face for the summit day and a look at the buttress the evening before; the cost is a 9-mile, 2,800 ft carry and a permit.

camps.name: Boulder Shelter — the last camp outside the national park
camps.why: A shorter 6-mile first day on free, no-booking ground with a roofed shelter; you then carry to Home Lake or the face boulders next morning.

new_camps.name: Home Lake
new_camps.why: The camp for this side of Inner Constance: a 9-mile walk in on maintained trail, then a summit day that returns to the same tents before the walk out.
new_camps.capacity: Lightly used sites on the wooded bluff above the western shore.
new_camps.permit: Overnight permit required (booked through Recreation.gov or the Port Angeles wilderness office); no campfires.
new_camps.notes: Sits a few hundred feet below Constance Pass, inside Olympic National Park. Boulder Shelter, about three miles lower, is the usual fallback for a late start.

camps.name: Lake Constance
camps.why: The only workable camp on this side: sites at the back of the lake put you at the foot of Avalanche Canyon, so the summit day starts from your tent.

camps.name: Lake Constance
camps.why: Every climb of the mountain starts here; designated sites at the back of the lake sit at the mouth of Avalanche Canyon, so you climb light and return to the same tent.

camps.name: Lake Constance — the standard base for the South Chute
camps.why: The base for every route on the mountain: designated sites at the north end of the lake, a toilet and bear wires on site, and the canyon starts a short walk away.

camps.name: Lake Constance — the standard base for the South Chute
camps.why: Two nights here let you carry the rack up on day one and climb the arete unburdened; the lake camp is the only legal base, and the canyon walk to the arete starts from it.

camps.name: Upper Lena Lake
camps.why: The easy first night: the last trail-side camp before the off-trail traverse, with lakeshore sites, so day two starts with fresh legs at the foot of the route.

camps.name: Lake of the Angels
camps.why: The end of the crux day: the only good camp on the south side of St. Peter's Gate, with a steep Putvin descent to the trailhead the next morning.

camps.name: Lena Lake designated sites
camps.why: A lower first night for a late start; it adds roughly 2,500 ft to day two and makes the traverse day very long, so most parties push to Upper Lena Lake.

camps.name: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
camps.why: Drive-in sites for the night before the hike; useful for a dawn start from the trailhead, but they add nothing during the trip itself.

plan_conflict: Lake of the Angels is on file as a route camp, but on this traverse it is where parties sleep on night 2, so it is listed as the main for that night.

camps.name: Lake of the Angels
camps.why: The only camp worth the steep Putvin climb: bare ground by the lake puts the summit within an afternoon or an early morning, with a short descent to the car after.

camps.name: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
camps.why: A drive-in option for the night before; lets you start the Putvin trail fresh and early, but it is not part of the trip's own nights.

plan_conflict: The plan puts the summit on day 2, but parties often climb Stone the afternoon they reach the lake and walk straight out the next day.

camps.name: Brothers base camp at Lena Forks
camps.why: The standard night: flat enough to sleep at, near water, and about 3,000 ft below the summit; it is deep forest, so expect shade and a wait for morning sun.

camps.name: Upper camp above the forks
camps.why: A small meadow near 3,600 ft that shortens the couloir day by a few hundred feet, but takes more route-finding and has fewer flat sites than the forks.

camps.name: Lower Lena Lake
camps.why: Only three miles in and about 1,000 ft lower than the usual camp; suits a late arrival, but leaves a very long summit day.

camps.name: The Brothers climbers camp, Valley of the Silent Men
camps.why: The standard high camp: at the foot of the south couloir, so the traverse day starts and ends here, and a second night is easy if the ridge goes slowly.

camps.name: Lena Lake designated sites
camps.why: Three easy miles from the road; a party starting after work can sleep here and carry the remaining three miles to the climbers camp in the morning.

camps.name: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
camps.why: Drive-in sites by the trailhead for the night before; they put you at the trail early, but you still sleep at the climbers camp on the trip.

plan_conflict: The plan has the climb and the walk-out on the same day; many parties instead sleep a second night at the climbers camp, because the traverse takes 10 to 12 hours.

camps.name: Boulder Shelter — the last camp outside the national park
camps.why: The camp most climbers use for Warrior Peak: a roofed shelter, water nearby, 6 miles in, no booking needed, and the cirque below the peak is a short morning walk above it.

camps.name: Home Lake, below Constance Pass — inside the park, and reached from the north
camps.why: About 400 ft of climbing and 3 miles beyond the shelter; it shaves the summit day but needs a permit and makes a longer day one.

camps.name: Camp Handy
camps.why: Three miles in on easy trail, free and sheltered; a spot for a late start, which leaves a very long day to the summit.

plan_conflict: The plan sleeps at Home Lake, but climbers mostly use Boulder Shelter for the night; Home Lake has been demoted to a route camp.

camps.name: Honeymoon Meadows
camps.why: The camp three-day parties use: a long established site with room for several tents; the summit push begins and ends here, though it makes a longer summit day.

camps.name: Tarn camp above Anderson Pass
camps.why: Open ground near water that cuts the summit day by hours; parties choose it for a shorter push or a two-night high camp, at the price of a long first day.

camps.name: Camp Siberia / Anderson Pass shelter area
camps.why: A sheltered camp in trees just below the pass that is easy to miss under snow; useful in bad weather, though it leaves the summit day long.

plan_conflict: The plan reaches the Anderson Pass tarn camp on day 1, but three-day parties usually stop at Honeymoon Meadows and climb from there.

camps.name: Cameron Basin
camps.why: The one camp zone for the climb: sites along the creek below the pass put the west ridge at your doorstep; bring a canister and fill water from the creek.

camps.name: Upper Royal Basin
camps.why: The climbers' camp: a mile above the lake, cutting the long summit day and giving the quickest access to Surprise Basin; the permit has to be booked by phone.

camps.name: Royal Lake
camps.why: The fallback when the upper-basin permit is not available: easier to book, ten sites, but 500 ft lower and a longer summit day.

camps.name: Lower Royal Meadow Camp
camps.why: A bare-ground camp below the lake for a late arrival; it leaves a very long day on day two.

plan_conflict: Royal Lake was on file as a main camp alongside Upper Royal Basin; only the upper basin is the main for this climb.

camps.name: Lost Basin camp
camps.why: The camp parties actually use: unmaintained sites at the head of the Lost River, a few hundred feet below the pass, so Claywood is a light day and the camp is quiet.

camps.name: Upper Cameron Basin high camp
camps.why: A shorter day one over Grand Pass, with a stream and many sites; the cost is another climb over Cameron Pass before the summit day.

camps.name: Dose Meadows
camps.why: The south-side base at the head of the Dosewallips; the washed-out road makes it a very long approach, so it is rarely used from Obstruction Point.

camps.name: Cameron Basin
camps.why: The staging camp for Cameron itself; sleeping here splits the Grand Pass day, but leaves the Lost Basin leg for the following day.

plan_conflict: Upper Cameron Basin and Dose Meadows were both main on file, but parties camp in Lost Basin for Claywood, as the plan says.

camps.name: Upper Royal Basin
camps.why: The climbers' camp, in sight of the couloir: most parties walk the extra mile above the lake so the summit day starts from tents at the foot of the route.

camps.name: Royal Lake
camps.why: The easier-to-book fallback when the upper basin is full; sites are plentiful, but the summit day starts 500 ft lower and runs longer.

plan_conflict: Royal Lake was a main camp on file next to Upper Royal Basin; research makes the upper basin the single main.

camps.name: Upper Royal Basin
camps.why: The climbers' camp: gravel flats beside the tarns put the Deception moraine right above you, and the basin has the best views and fewest bugs.

camps.name: Royal Lake
camps.why: The fallback when the upper-basin permit is gone: more sites and an easier booking, but a mile and 500 ft farther from the climb.

camps.name: Royal Creek
camps.why: Forested sites well short of the basin; only for a very late arrival, since it adds hours to the summit day.

camps.name: Lower Royal Meadow
camps.why: A bare-ground meadow just below the lake that fills in when the lake is booked; costs a little height on summit day.

plan_conflict: Royal Lake was a main camp on file next to Upper Royal Basin; only the upper basin is the main.

camps.name: Home Lake
camps.why: The camp for this side of Fricaba: a few hundred feet below Constance Pass, so the Deception Basin day starts close to the route; a permit is required.

camps.name: Camp Handy
camps.why: Three miles in, free and sheltered; a first-night stop for a late start, but it leaves a long walk and big climb before the summit day.

camps.name: Boulder Shelter
camps.why: Six miles in at the trail junction; a roofed, no-permit fallback when Home Lake is full, and one climb shorter on the day out.

plan_conflict: Most parties climb Fricaba from a camp in Deception Basin on the Royal Basin side, not from Home Lake.
